newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Oil deal extension assures Gulf War claim payout.
newsitem.headline: Oil deal extension assures Gulf War claim payout.

text.p: Some 220,000 Gulf War victims will likely receive $557 million in August following the Security Council's renewal of the oil-for-food deal with Iraq, the head of the United Nations reparations fund said on Thursday.

Jean-Claude Aime, executive secretary of the U.N. Compensation Commission, also told Reuters he hoped a similar amount could be paid out to another large batch of claimants around year-end -- if the deal is rolled over again.

The Geneva-based fund, the largest reparations scheme ever, was set up by the Security Council after the Gulf War in 1991 to compensate losses directly caused by Iraq's invasion of Kuwait and its seven-month occupation of the oil-rich emirate.

It receives 30 per cent of the revenue (or $100 million a month) from the limited sale of Iraqi crude oil, which the Security Council extended on Wednesday for another six months to ease the plight of Iraqi civilians under crippling sanctions.
"We're very pleased with this decision of the Council," Aime told Reuters. "This will enable the Compensation Commission to continue its activities and make payments in August.
"We expect to make the next payment of $557 million in August and probably another one in December or January on that order," added Aime.

Under the current plan, which expires on June 7, Iraq has been allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil to buy food, medicine and other necessities to help alleviate the effects of embargoes in force since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The resolution, voted unanimously, would renew the arrangement for another 180-day period from June 8.

The August payout is expected to be approved later this month by the Compensation Commission's Governing Council, according to Aime and diplomats. Composed of the same 15 members as the Security Council, it is due to meet from June 23-24.
"We hope the (Governing) Council will give its green light," Aime said. "It is more or less on track."
Aime, who is Haitian, took over from Carlos Alzamora, a former Peruvian diplomat who retired in January.

The fund's first major payout was last March when it transferred $144 million to 57,636 claimants who proved they had been forced to leave Kuwait or Iraq, or had lost up to $100,000 in personal property.
The 222,000 claimants to receive compensation in August are also in the categories of "forced departure" or those with losses of up to $100,000. Each will be paid $2,500.
"It is much easier to work when the money is coming in," Aime said.
"At the same time, this raises expectations on the part of claimants who would like to see their claims processed rapidly and the money coming in their direction," he added.
The Compensation Commission has received 2.6 million claims worth $220 billion from individuals, companies and governments for losses allegedly caused by Iraq.
The Governing Council, which has ruled that individual claimants get priority, previously paid out $13.4 million to 4,000 claimants who proved serious personal injury or death of a close relative.
Funded largely by donations and seized Iraqi assets, its coffers were nearly empty until the oil-for-food deal finally went through last December.
